Epistle

Here begins the epistle of Saint Jerome to the priest Paulinus concerning all the books of divine history. Chapter One.

Brother Ambrose, bringing me your little gifts, delivered them along with a most delightful letter, which from the beginning proved friendships of faith and long-standing acquaintance. For that true bond—glued together with the cement of Christ—is not the practical usefulness of household affairs, not mere bodily presence, not deceitful and flattering praise, but the fear of God and the study of the divine Scriptures unite it. We read in ancient histories that certain men traveled through provinces, visited new peoples, crossed seas, so that those whom they knew from books they might also see face to face. Thus Pythagoras traveled most laboriously among the prophets of Memphis; thus Plato traveled through Egypt and to Archytas of Tarentum, and to that shore of Italy which was once called Magna Graecia; so that one who was a master at Athens, and powerful, whose teachings resounded through the schools of the Academy, became a wanderer and a pupil, preferring to learn modestly from others rather than impose his own views shamelessly. Finally, when he pursues letters as if fleeing throughout the whole world, captured by pirates and sold into slavery, he served a most cruel tyrant; led captive, bound, and a slave—yet because he was a philosopher, he was greater than the one who bought him. We read that to Livy, flowing with a fountain of milk-white eloquence, certain nobles came from the farthest borders of Spain and Gaul—men whom Rome itself had not drawn to behold, but whom the fame of one man had led there. That age possessed a miracle unheard of in all ages, worthy of celebration: that having entered so great a city, they sought something else outside the city.

Apollonius, whether that magician as the common people say, or philosopher as the Pythagoreans hold, entered Persia, crossed the Caucasus, the Albanians, Scythians, Massagetae, penetrated the wealthiest kingdoms of India; and finally, having crossed the vast river Physon, came to the Brahmans, so that he might hear Hyarcas teaching, seated on a golden throne and drinking from the fountain of Tantalus, among a few disciples, about nature, about morals, and about the course of days and stars. From there, through the Elamites, Babylonians, Chaldeans, Medes, Assyrians, Parthians, Syrians, Phoenicians, Arabs, Palestinians, he returned to Alexandria, and proceeded to Ethiopia, so that he might see the Gymnosophists and the famous Table of the Sun in the sand. That man found everywhere something to learn, and always advancing, always made himself better. Philostratus wrote most fully about this in eight volumes. Chapter 2.

What shall I say of the men of this world, when the apostle Paul, the chosen vessel and teacher of the nations, who spoke of the testimony of so great a guest within himself, saying: 'Do you seek proof of him who speaks in me, Christ?'—after Damascus and Arabia had been explored, went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days. For by this mystery of the week and the eighth day, he who was to be the preacher to the Gentiles had to be instructed. And again, after fourteen years, taking Barnabas and Titus, he laid before the apostles the Gospel he preached, lest perhaps he should run or have run in vain. There is something of hidden energy in the living voice: and what is poured from the author's own mouth into the ears of the disciple sounds more forcefully. Whence also Aeschines, when driven out to Rhodes, and reading there the speeches of Demosthenes...

...the speech which he had spoken against him, all marveling and praising him, he said with a sigh, 'What if you had heard that beast itself resounding its own words?'

He does not say this because there is anything of such a kind in me that you could hear from me or wish to learn; but because your ardor and zeal for learning ought to be proven even without us, by itself. A teachable nature is praiseworthy even without a teacher. It is not what you may find, but what you seek that we consider. Wax is soft and easily shaped; even if the hands of the craftsman and modeler are absent, still by its own virtue it can become whatever it may be. The Apostle Paul boasts that he learned the Law of Moses and the Prophets at the feet of Gamaliel, so that, armed with spiritual weapons, he might afterward teach with confidence. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God for the destruction of fortifications and for destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ, and being ready to subdue all disobedience. He writes that Timothy was instructed in the sacred letters from infancy, and exhorts him to the study of reading, not to neglect the grace that was given to him through the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Elsewhere he commands that among the other virtues of a bishop, which he describes in brief words, he should not neglect the Scriptures; 'holding fast,' he says, 'the faithful word as he has been taught, that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to convince the gainsayers.'

Indeed, holy rusticity profits only itself, and inasmuch as it builds up the Church of Christ by its way of life, so much does it harm if it does not resist those who destroy it. The prophet Malachi—or rather the Lord through Malachi—questioned the priests about the Law. It is the office of the priest, when questioned, to answer concerning the Law. And in Deuteronomy we read: 'Ask your father and he will declare to you; your elders, and they will tell you.' In the one hundred eighteenth Psalm: 'Your testimonies have been my songs in the place of my pilgrimage.' And in the description of the just man, when he compares him to the tree of life, David also included this among his other virtues: 'His will is in the law of the Lord, and in His law he will meditate day and night.' Daniel, at the end of his most sacred vision, says: 'The just shall shine as stars, and the wise'—that is, the learned—'as the firmament.' See how far apart uneducated simplicity and learned righteousness are from one another. Some are compared to stars, others to the sky itself. Although, according to the Hebrew truth, either may be understood of the learned. For thus we read among them: those who have been learned shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like the stars unto perpetual eternities. Why does Paul the Apostle call himself a 'vessel of election'? Surely because he was a vessel of the Law, and the storehouse of the holy Scriptures. The Pharisees are astonished at the Lord's teaching, and marvel at Peter and John, how they know the Law, since they had not learned letters. Whatever daily practice and meditation on the Law usually supplies to others, the Holy Spirit was suggesting to them in its own time.

And it was according to what is written: 'They shall be taught of God.'

The Savior had completed twelve years, and sitting in the temple, questioning about matters of the Law, He teaches more than He, as a prudent inquirer, asks. Unless perhaps we should call Peter and John rustic fishermen—each of whom could speak, and although unskilled in speech, not in knowledge. John was rustic, a fisherman by training. Which all everywhere claim as their own. We write, unlearned and learned alike, poems everywhere. A garrulous old woman, a doting old man, a wordy sophist – all of these, presuming to lay hold of it, tear at it before they have learned it. Some, with raised eyebrows, weigh grand words, philosophizing about the sacred letters among little women. Others learn – shame to say – from women what they should be teaching men; and lest this seem too little, with a certain facility of words, or rather audacity, they teach others what they themselves do not understand. I say nothing of those like myself who, if they happen to come to the sacred scriptures after secular literature, and their ears are charmed by a well-composed style, think that whatever they say is the law of God. They do not deign to know what the prophets or apostles meant, but adapt incongruous testimonies to their own meaning – as though it were a great thing, and not the most vicious kind of speaking, to pervert sentences and to drag the sacred scripture, resisting them, to their own will. As if we had not read the Homeric centos and Virgilian centos, and as if we could not, in the same way, call Maro a Christian without Christ – because he wrote 'now returns the virgin, the reign of Saturn returns; now a new offspring is sent down from heaven above.' And the father speaking to the son: 'My son, my strength, my great power, alone.' And after the words of the Savior on the cross: 'Recalling such things, he remained fixed.' These are childish things, and like the games of jugglers – to teach what you do not know; indeed, to speak with disgust, not even to know that you do not know. 

And its own precepts. In brief is the book of Leviticus, in which each single sacrifice, indeed each single word, and the vestments of Aaron and the order of the Levitical priesthood breathe heavenly sacraments. Numbers indeed contains the whole of arithmetic, and the prophecy of Balaam, and the forty-two stations through the wilderness that mark out mysteries. Deuteronomy truly is a second copy of the law and a foreshadowing of the Gospel law – does it not so contain those things which are first, that they may all be made new? Concerning the old – thus far Moses, thus far the Pentateuch – of which the Apostle boasts that he is able to speak in the Church in five words. Job is an example of patience, which embraces no small mysteries in its own discourse. It begins in prose, proceeds in verse, and ends in prose-style speech; and it determines all the laws of dialectic – proposition, assumption, confirmation, refutation. Each single word is full of meanings; and, that I may be silent about the rest, concerning the resurrection of the body it speaks so clearly that no one has written of it more plainly or more carefully. He says: 'I know that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise again from the earth; and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another's. This my hope is laid up in my bosom.' I come to Joshua, the son of Nun, who bears the type of the Lord's name not only in his deeds but also in his very name. He crossed the Jordan, overthrew the kingdoms of the enemies, divided the land among the victorious people; and through each city, town, mountain, river, torrent, and boundary, describes the spiritual kingdoms of the heavenly Jerusalem and its Church. In the book of Judges, how many are the leaders, so many are the figures. Ruth the Moabite fulfills the prophecy of Isaiah, saying: 'Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, the ruler of the earth; from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.' Samuel, at the death of Eli and in the rejection of Saul, abolishes the old law.

Et per hos disseminati sunt populi chananeorum. Factique sunt termini chanaan venientibus a sydone versus geram usque gazam donec ingrediaris sodomam et gomorram et adamam et seboim usque lesa. Hii sunt filii cham in cognationibus et linguis et generationibus terrisque et gentibus suis. De sem quoque nati sunt patre omnium filiorum heber fratre iaphet maiore. Filii sem: helam et assur et arphaxat et lud et aram. Filii aram: hus et hul et gether et mes. At vero arphaxat genuit sale de quo ortus est heber. Natique sunt heber filii duo. Nomen uni phaleg: eo quod in diebus eius divisa sit terra: et nomen fratris eius iectan. Qui iectan genuit elmodad et saleph et asarmoth iare et aduram et uzal et decla et hebal et abimahel saba et ophir et evila et iobab. Omnes isti filii iectan. Et facta est habitatio eorum de mesa pergentibus usque sephar montem orientalem. Isti filii sem secundum cognationes et linguas et regiones in gentibus suis. Haec familiae noe iuxta populos et nationes suas. Ab hijs divise sunt gentes in terra post diluvium.

He took all these and divided them in the middle, and set each half opposite the other; but the birds he did not divide. And birds came down upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away. And as the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and a great and dark horror seized him. And it was said to him: Know for certain that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own, and they shall bring them into servitude and afflict them four hundred years. But I will judge the nation whom they will serve; and afterward they will go out with great possessions. But you shall go to your fathers in peace, buried in a good old age. But in the fourth generation they shall return here, for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet completed... to the present time. After this a man went out (chapter 2) from the house of Levi, and took a wife of his own kindred, who conceived and bore a son; and seeing him goodly, she hid him three months. And when she could no longer hide him, she took a basket of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and pitch, and put the infant inside, and set it in the sedge by the river's bank, his sister standing afar off to see what would happen. And behold, Pharaoh's daughter came down to wash herself in the river, and her maidens walked along the river's brink. When she had seen the basket among the reeds, she sent one of her maids to fetch it; and opening it, and seeing within it a crying babe, she took pity on him and said: This is one of the Hebrews' children. Then his sister said: Shall I go and call to you a Hebrew woman to nurse the child? She answered: Go. The girl went and called the child's mother. To whom Pharaoh's daughter said: Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages. The woman took the child and nursed him; and when he was grown she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter. And she adopted him as a son, and called his name Moses, saying: Because I drew him out of the water. In those days, after Moses had grown up, he went out to his brethren, and saw their affliction, and an Egyptian smiting one of the Hebrews, his brethren. And when he had looked this way and that, and saw no one, he struck the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. And going out the next day, he saw two Hebrews fighting, and said to him who did the wrong: Why do you strike your fellow? He answered: Who made you a ruler and judge over us? Do you mean to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday? Moses was afraid, and said: How is this thing known? And Pharaoh heard of this matter and sought to kill Moses. But he, fleeing from Pharaoh's presence, dwelt in the land of Midian, and sat down by a well. Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, who came to draw water, and having filled the troughs, wished to water their father's flocks. But shepherds came and drove them away. Then Moses arose and defended the girls and watered their sheep. When they returned to Jethro their father, he said to them: Why have you come so soon today? They said: An Egyptian delivered us from the hand of the shepherds, and moreover he drew water for us and gave the flock to drink. He said: Where is he? Why did you leave the man? Call him, that he may eat bread. So Moses swore to dwell with him. And he took Zipporah his daughter to wife, who bore him a son whom he called Gershom, saying: I have been a stranger in a foreign land. [You shall not] carry out of it [the meat] outside; nor shall you break its bone. All the assembly of the children of Israel shall do it. And if any of the foreigners among you wish to pass over and keep the Passover of the Lord, first let every male of his be circumcised, and then he may celebrate it in the proper manner, and he shall be as one born in the land; but no uncircumcised person shall eat of it. The same law shall be for the native and for the stranger who sojourns among you. And all the children of Israel did as the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron; and on the same day the Lord brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their companies. Chapter 13.

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Sanctify to me every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and of beast; they are mine, for all are mine. And Moses said to the people: Remember this day in which you went out from Egypt, out of the house of bondage, for by a mighty hand the Lord brought you out from this place; therefore you shall not eat leavened bread. Today you go out in the month of new grain. And when the Lord shall have brought you into the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall keep this manner of service in this month. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day shall be a solemnity of the Lord. Unleavened bread shall you eat seven days; nothing leavened shall be seen with you, nor in all your borders. And you shall tell your son in that day, saying: This is what the Lord did for me when I came out of Egypt. And it shall be as a sign to you upon your hand, and as a memorial before your eyes, that the law of the Lord may always be in your mouth; for by a mighty hand the Lord brought you out of Egypt. Therefore you shall observe this rite at its appointed time, from days to days. And when the Lord shall have brought you into the land of the Canaanite,

as he swore to you and your fathers, and shall have given it to you, you shall set apart to the Lord all that opens the womb, and whatever is firstborn among your cattle; whatever is male, you shall consecrate to the Lord. Every firstling of an ass you shall exchange for a sheep; and if you do not redeem it, you shall kill it. Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem with a price. And when your son shall ask you tomorrow, saying, What is this?, you shall answer him: By a mighty hand the Lord brought us out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. For when Pharaoh was hardened and would not let us go, the Lord killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of man to the firstborn of beast. Therefore I sacrifice to the Lord every male that opens the womb, and I redeem all the firstborn of my sons. And it shall be as a sign upon your hand, and as a thing hung between your eyes, as a memorial, because by a mighty hand the Lord brought you out of Egypt. And when Pharaoh had sent forth the people, the Lord did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, though it was near, thinking that perhaps the people might repent when they saw wars arise against them, and might return into Egypt; but he led them about by the way of the desert that is by the Red Sea. And the children of Israel went up armed out of the land of Egypt. And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, because he had made the children of Israel swear, saying: God will visit you; carry my bones from here with you. And setting forth from Succoth, they camped in Etham, in the edge of the wilderness. And the Lord went before them to show the way, by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire, that he might be the guide of their journey at both times. The pillar of cloud never failed by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, before the people.

...whether standing crops in the fields: he who kindled the fire shall repay the damage. If a man commit money or vessels to his friend to keep, and they be stolen from him that received them, if the thief be found, he shall repay double. If the thief be not known, the master of the house shall be brought before the gods (judges), and shall swear that he did not lay his hand upon his neighbor's goods to commit fraud, whether it be about an ox, an ass, a sheep, or a garment, or anything that may cause damage. The cause of both parties shall come before the gods (judges), and he whom they condemn shall restore double to his neighbor. If a man deliver to his neighbor an ox, an ass, a sheep, or any beast to keep, and it die or be hurt or be taken away by enemies, and no man saw it, there shall be an oath between them that he did not put his hand to his neighbor's goods; and the owner shall accept the oath, and he shall not be compelled to make restitution. But if it were stolen from him, he shall make restitution to the owner. If it were devoured by a wild beast, let him bring what was killed and he shall not make restitution. If a man borrow anything of his neighbor, and it be hurt or die, the owner not being present, he shall be compelled to make restitution. But if the owner be present, he shall not make restitution, especially if it was hired for its work. If a man deceive a virgin not yet betrothed, and lie with her, he shall endow her, and have her as wife. If her father refuse to give her, he shall pay money according to the dowry which virgins are wont to receive. Thou shalt not suffer wizards to live. Whosoever copulateth with a beast shall be put to death. He that sacrificeth to gods, save to the Lord only, shall be slain. Thou shalt not molest a stranger, nor afflict him, for you also were strangers in the land of Egypt. You shall not harm a widow or an orphan. If you hurt them, they will cry out to me, and I will hear their cry, and my wrath will be indignant, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall be widows and your children fatherless. If you lend money to my poor people who dwell with you, you shall not oppress them as a usurer, nor exact interest. If you take your neighbor's garment as a pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun sets, for it is his only covering, wherewith he covers his body, and he has nothing else to sleep in. If he cries to me, I will hear him, for I am merciful. You shall not speak ill of the gods, and you shall not curse the ruler of your people. You shall not delay to offer your tithes and first-fruits. You shall give me the firstborn of your sons; likewise of your oxen and sheep. Seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day you shall give it to me. You shall be holy men to me. Flesh that has been torn by beasts you shall not eat, but shall throw it to the dogs.

Moses saw that the people were naked, for Aaron had stripped them for a disgrace among their enemies, and had left them naked. And standing at the gate of the camp, he said: If any man be on the Lord's side, let him join with me. And all the sons of Levi gathered themselves to him. And he said to them: Thus saith the Lord God of Israel: Put every man his sword upon his thigh: go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let every man kill his brother, and friend, and neighbour. And the sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses, and there fell of the people that day about twenty-three thousand men. And Moses said: You have consecrated your hands this day to the Lord, every man in his son and in his brother, that a blessing may be given to you. And the next day Moses spoke to the people: You have sinned a very great sin. I will go up to the Lord: if by any means I may be able to entreat him for your crime. And returning to the Lord, he said: I beseech thee, Lord, this people hath sinned a heinous sin, and they have made to themselves gods of gold: either forgive them this trespass, or if thou do not, strike me out of the book that thou hast written. And the Lord answered him: He that hath sinned against me, him will I strike out of my book. But go thou, and lead this people whither I have told thee: my angel shall go before thee. And in the day of vengeance I will visit this sin also of theirs. And the Lord struck the people for the guilt of the calf which Aaron had made. Chapter 33.

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Go, get thee up from this place, thou and thy people whom thou hast brought out of the land of Egypt, into the land which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying: To thy seed I will give it. And I will send a precursor angel before thee, that I may cast out the Canaanite, and the Amorite, and the Hittite, and the Perizzite, and the Hivite, and the Jebusite, and thou mayst enter into the land flowing with milk and honey.

...upon it, which had been rightly commanded. The candlestick shall stand with its lamps, and the golden altar on which incense is burned before the ark of the testimony. You shall place the hanging at the entrance of the tabernacle of the testimony, and before it the altar of holocaust. The laver shall be between the altar and the tabernacle, which you shall fill with water. You shall enclose the court with its hangings and its entrance. And taking the oil of unction, you shall anoint the tabernacle with its vessels so that they may be sanctified: the altar of holocaust and all its vessels; the laver with its base. You shall consecrate all things with the oil of anointing, that they may be most holy. You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the doors of the tabernacle of the testimony, and having washed them with water, you shall clothe them with holy garments, that they may minister to me, and that their anointing may advance to an everlasting priesthood. And Moses did all things which the Lord had commanded. So in the first month of the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was set up. And Moses raised it up and placed the boards, bases, and bars; he set up the pillars, and spread the roof over the tabernacle, putting a covering above it, as the Lord had commanded. He also placed the testimony in the ark, putting the bars beneath it, and the mercy seat above. And when he had brought the ark into the tabernacle of the testimony, he hung a veil before it to fulfill the Lord's command. He also placed the table in the tabernacle of the testimony, on the north side, outside the veil, arranging before it the loaves of proposition, as the Lord had commanded Moses. He also placed the candlestick in the tabernacle of the testimony opposite the table, on the south side, arranging the lamps in order according to the Lord's command. ...in the tabernacle of testimony. The rest of the blood he shall pour out beside the base of the altar of holocausts, which is at the door of the tabernacle of testimony. And he shall take away all its fat and burn it upon the altar, doing thus as he did with the previous bullock; and the priest praying for them, the Lord will be merciful to them. But the bullock itself he shall carry forth outside the camp and burn it, as he did the former bullock, because it is for the sin of the multitude. If a prince shall sin and do one thing of many through ignorance, which the law of the Lord forbids, and afterward shall understand his sin, he shall offer a sacrifice to the Lord, a he-goat without blemish, and shall lay his hand upon its head. And when he has immolated it in the place where the holocaust is usually slain before the Lord, because it is for sin, the priest shall dip his finger in the blood of the victim for sin, touching the horns of the altar of holocaust, and shall pour the rest at the base of it; but the fat he shall burn above as is usually done in peace offerings. And the priest shall pray for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him. But if a soul shall sin through ignorance from among the people of the land, doing any of those things which are forbidden by the law of the Lord, and shall offend and know his sin, he shall offer a she-goat without blemish, and shall lay his hands upon the head of the victim which is for sin, and shall immolate it in the place of the holocaust. And the priest shall take of the blood on his finger, and touching the horns of the altar of holocaust, shall pour out the rest at its base. And taking away all the fat, as is usually taken from the victims of peace offerings, he shall burn it upon the altar for a sweet odor to the Lord; and he shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him. But if he shall offer of the flocks a victim for sin, namely an unblemished ewe...

he shall lay his hand upon its head, and shall immolate it in the place where the victims of holocausts are usually slain. And the priest shall take of its blood with his finger and touch the horns of the altar of holocaust, and shall pour out the rest at its base. And taking away all the fat, as the fat of the ram which is offered for peace offerings is usually taken away, he shall burn it upon the altar as an incense to the Lord; and he shall pray for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him. Chapter 5.

If a soul shall sin, and having heard the voice of one swearing, and being a witness that he either saw or was privy to it, does not disclose it, he shall bear his iniquity. The soul that touches anything unclean, whether it be that which was killed by a beast, or died of itself, or any other creeping thing, and forgets its uncleanness, is guilty and has offended; and if he touches anything of the uncleanness of man, according to any impurity by which one is usually defiled, and having forgotten it afterward comes to know it, he shall be liable for the guilt. The soul that swears and utters with his lips that he would do evil or good, and does not do it, and afterward, forgetting his oath, comes to understand his sin, let him do penance for his sin and offer of the flocks a lamb or a she-goat; and the priest shall pray for him and for his sins. But if he cannot offer a beast, let him offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the Lord, one for sin and the other for a holocaust; and he shall give them to the priest. Who, offering first that which is for sin, shall wring its head back near the little wings, so that it cleaves to the neck and is not entirely broken off, and shall sprinkle the wall of the altar with its blood. And whatever remains he shall let drip down to the foundation of the altar, because it is for sin. But the other he shall burn as a holocaust as is customary; and the priest shall pray for him.

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: If a man make a vow, and promise his soul to God, he shall give the price according to estimation. If it be a male, from the twentieth year to the sixtieth year, he shall give fifty shekels of silver, according to the measure of the sanctuary: if a woman, thirty. But from the fifth year to the twentieth, a male shall give twenty shekels; a female, ten. From one month to five years old, for a male shall be given five shekels; for a female, three. Sixty years old and upward, a male shall give fifteen shekels; a female, ten. But if he be poor and unable to pay the estimation, he shall stand before the priest, and as much as he shall value him and see that he is able to pay, so much shall he give. But an animal that may be sacrificed to the Lord, if any man vow it, shall be holy, and cannot be changed: that is, neither a better for a worse, nor a worse for a better. And if he change it, both the one that was changed, and that for which it was changed, shall be consecrated to the Lord. An unclean animal, which may not be sacrificed to the Lord, if any man vow it, shall be brought before the priest, who, judging whether it be good or bad, shall set the price. But if he that offers wishes to redeem it, he shall add a fifth part above the estimation. If a man vow his house...

and sanctify it to the Lord, the priest shall consider it, whether it be good or bad, and it shall be sold according to the price which the priest shall have fixed. But if he that vowed it wishes to redeem it, he shall give a fifth part above the estimation, and shall have the house. But if he vow and consecrate to the Lord a field of his possession, the price shall be estimated according to the measure of seed. If the land is sown with thirty measures of barley, it shall be sold for fifty shekels of silver. But if some time after, the priest shall reckon the money according to the number of years that remain until the jubilee, and it shall be deducted from the price. But if he will not redeem it, but it is sold to another, he who vowed it can no longer redeem it: for when the jubilee comes, the day shall be sanctified to the Lord, and the consecrated possession belongs to the priests by right. All who were numbered in the camp of Judah were one hundred eighty-six thousand four hundred: and by their companies they shall march out first. In the camp of the sons of Reuben, toward the south, the prince shall be Elisur son of Sedeur: and the whole army of fighting men numbered was forty-six thousand five hundred. In the tribe of Gad the prince was Eliasaph son of Duel: and the whole army of fighting men numbered was forty-five thousand six hundred fifty. All who were mustered in the camp of Reuben: one hundred fifty-one thousand four hundred fifty: they shall set out in the second place by their companies. The tabernacle of the testimony shall be carried by the offices of the Levites, and their companies. As it is raised, so shall it be taken down. Each shall proceed in their own places and order. Toward the west shall be the camp of the sons of Ephraim: whose prince was Helisama son of Ammiud. The whole army of his fighting men numbered: forty thousand five hundred. Abidan son of Gedeon: and the whole army of his fighting men mustered: thirty-five thousand four hundred. Next to him the tribe of Asher pitched their tents: whose prince was Phegiel son of Ochran. The whole army of his fighting men numbered: forty-one thousand five hundred. Of the tribe of the sons of Naphtali the prince was Ahira son of Enan. The whole army of his fighting men: fifty-three thousand four hundred. All who were numbered in the camp of Dan: were one hundred fifty-seven thousand six hundred: and they shall march last. But when you make a holocaust or a sacrifice of oxen to fulfill a vow or as peace offerings, you shall give for each ox three-tenths of flour sprinkled with oil, which shall be half a hin of measure, and wine for libations poured of the same measure, as an offering of most sweet odor to the Lord. Thus shall you do for each ox and ram and lamb and kid, whether native or sojourner, they shall offer sacrifices by the same rite. There shall be one law and one judgment for you and for the sojourners of the land. The Lord spoke to Moses saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them. When you have come into the land which I will give you, and shall eat of the bread of that region, you shall separate first-fruits to the Lord from your foods. As you separate first-fruits from the threshing floors, so also from your dough you shall give first-fruits to the Lord. But if through ignorance you shall have omitted any of these things which the Lord spoke to Moses, and commanded through him to you, from the day he began to command and onward, and the multitude shall have forgotten to do it: they shall offer a bull from the herd as a holocaust of most sweet odor to the Lord, and its sacrifice and libations as the ceremonies require, and a he-goat for sin: and the priest shall pray for the whole multitude of the children of Israel, and it shall be forgiven them, since they sinned not willingly, nevertheless offering incense to the Lord for themselves and for their sin and error, and it shall be forgiven the whole people of the children of Israel, and the sojourners who dwell among you: since the fault is of all the people through ignorance. But if one soul shall sin unknowingly, she shall offer a yearling she-goat for her sin: and the priest shall pray for her that she sinned unknowingly before the Lord; and he shall obtain pardon for her, and it shall be forgiven her. There shall be one law for the native and for the sojourner, for all who sin through ignorance. But the soul that shall commit anything through pride, whether a citizen or a stranger, since he has rebelled against the Lord, shall perish from his people. For he has despised the word of the Lord, and made void his commandment: therefore he shall be destroyed and shall bear his iniquity. They shut him up in prison, not knowing what they ought to do with him. And the Lord said to Moses: Let that man die the death: let all the crowd stone him outside the camp. And when they had brought him out, they stoned him with stones: and he died, as the Lord had commanded. The Lord also said to Moses: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: That they make themselves fringes on the corners of their garments, putting in them ribbons of blue. They shall possess nothing else, being content with the offering of tithes, which I have separated for their use and their necessities. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command and declare to the Levites: When you have received from the sons of Israel the tithes which I have given you, offer their firstfruits to the Lord, that is, a tenth part of the tithe, so that it may be reckoned to you as an offering of firstfruits, both from the threshing floors and from the winepresses. And of whatever you receive as firstfruits, offer to the Lord, and give it to Aaron the priest. All that you offer from the tithes and set apart as gifts to the Lord shall be the best and choicest. And say to them: If you offer the fat and better portions from the tithes, it shall be reckoned to you as though you had given the firstfruits from the threshing floor and winepress; and you shall eat them in all your places, both you and your households, for it is your wage for the ministry by which you serve in the tabernacle of the testimony; and you shall not sin in this regard by reserving for yourselves the choice and fat portions, lest you defile the offerings of the children of Israel and die. Chapter 19.

And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the ordinance of the victim which the Lord has appointed. Command the sons of Israel that they bring to you a red heifer of perfect age, in which there is no blemish, and which has not borne the yoke; and you shall give it to Eleazar the priest. Having led it outside the camp, he shall immolate it in the sight of all; and dipping his finger in its blood, he shall sprinkle it seven times toward the front of the tabernacle, and shall burn it in the sight of all: its skin and flesh and blood together with its dung shall be delivered to the flame.

[Right column, continuing chapter 19:] Also cedar wood and hyssop, and scarlet twice dyed, the priest shall cast into the flame that devours the heifer. And afterward, having washed his clothes and body with water, he shall go out into the camp, and shall be unclean until evening. But he also who burns it shall wash his garments and body, and shall be unclean until evening. And a clean man shall gather up the ashes of the heifer, and pour them out outside the camp in a very clean place, that they may be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel, for the water of sprinkling, because it is for sin: the heifer having been burnt for sin. And whoever gathers the ashes of the heifer shall wash his garments, and shall be unclean until evening. This shall be a perpetual ordinance for the children of Israel and for those who dwell among them. Whoever touches the corpse of a man, and for this reason shall be unclean for seven days, shall be sprinkled with this water on the third day and on the seventh, and so shall be cleansed. If he is not sprinkled on the third day, he cannot be purified on the seventh. Whoever touches the corpse of a human soul, and is not sprinkled with this mixture, defiles the tabernacle of the Lord, and shall be cut off from Israel. Because the water of purification has not been sprinkled upon him, he shall be unclean, and his uncleanness shall remain upon him. This is the law for a man who dies in the tent. And they gave a thousand men from each of the tribes, that is twelve thousand armed for battle: whom Moses sent with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest; and he gave into his hand the holy vessels and the trumpets to sound. And when they had fought against the Midianites and had prevailed, they killed all the males and their kings—Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, five princes of the nation. They also killed Balaam the son of Beor with the sword; and they took captive their women and children and all their cattle and all their household goods. Whatever they were able to possess they laid waste, both cities and villages, and burned the fortresses with fire. And they carried off the plunder and everything they had taken, both of men and of beasts, and brought it to Moses and Eleazar the priest and to the whole assembly of the children of Israel. They also brought the rest of the goods to the camp in the plains of Moab, by the Jordan opposite Jericho.

And Moses and Eleazar the priest and all the leaders of the congregation went out to meet them outside the camp. And Moses, being angry with the officers of the army, the tribunes and centurions who had come from the war, said: 'Why have you spared the women? Are not these the ones who deceived the children of Israel, at the suggestion of Balaam, and caused you to sin against the Lord in the matter of Peor, on account of which the people were struck? Therefore kill all of them. Whoever is male, even among the little ones, and the women who have known a man by lying with him, kill; but keep for yourselves the girls and all the women who are virgins. And remain outside the camp for seven days. Whoever kills a man, or touches one slain, shall be purified on the third day and the seventh. And every plunder, whether it be clothing or a vessel or anything prepared for use, made of goats' skins, or hair, or wood, shall be purified.'

Eleazar the priest also spoke thus to the men of the army who had fought: 'This is the ordinance of the law which the Lord commanded Moses: Gold and silver and bronze and iron and lead and tin, and everything that can pass through the flames, shall be purified by fire; but whatever cannot endure fire shall be purified with the water of purification. And you shall wash your garments on the seventh day, and being purified afterward you shall enter the camp.'

The Lord also said to Moses: 'Take the sum of what has been captured, from man to beast, you and Eleazar the priest and the leaders of the people; and you shall divide the spoil equally between those who fought and went out to battle and the rest of the whole multitude. And you shall set apart a portion for the Lord from those who fought and were in the battle: one soul out of every five hundred, whether of men or oxen or donkeys or sheep; and you shall give it to Eleazar the priest, because they are the firstfruits of the Lord. And from the other half belonging to the children of Israel you shall take one out of every fifty, of men and oxen and donkeys and sheep and all animals, and give them to the Levites who keep watch over the tabernacle of the Lord.'

And Moses and Eleazar did as the Lord had commanded. Now the spoil which the army had taken was: six hundred seventy-five thousand sheep; seventy-two thousand oxen; sixty-one thousand donkeys; and thirty-two thousand persons of the female sex who had not known men. And Moses gave the number of the firstlings of the LORD to Eleazar the priest, as had been commanded him, from the half part of the children of Israel which he had separated for those who had been in the battle. And of the other half part which had fallen to the rest of the multitude, that is, of thirty-seven thousand five hundred, and of the oxen thirty-six thousand, and of the asses thirty thousand five hundred, and of the persons sixteen thousand — Moses took the fiftieth head and gave it to the Levites who kept the watch of the tabernacle of the LORD, as the LORD had commanded. And when the captains of the army, and the tribunes and centurions, had come to Moses, they said: We your servants have taken the number of the fighting men whom we had under our hand, and not one of them is missing. Therefore we offer as a gift to the LORD, each what he could find of gold in the spoil — anklets, bracelets, rings, armlets, and necklaces — that you might pray for us to the LORD. And Moses and Eleazar the priest received all the gold in its various kinds, weighing sixteen thousand seven hundred fifty shekels, from the tribunes and centurions. Each had what he had taken as spoil for himself. And that which was received they brought into the tabernacle of the testimony, as a memorial for the children of Israel before the LORD. Now the children of Reuben and Gad had a great multitude of cattle: and they had exceedingly abundant substance in livestock. And when they saw that Jazer and Gilead were lands suited for the raising of animals, they came to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the leaders of the multitude, and said: Ataroth, and Dibon, and Jazer, and Nimrah, Heshbon,

and Elealeh, and Sebam, and Nebo, and Beon — the land which the LORD struck down before the children of Israel — is a region exceedingly good for pasture of cattle: and we your servants have very many livestock; and we beg, if we have found favor in your sight, that you give this land to us your servants as a possession, and do not make us cross the Jordan. To whom Moses replied: Shall your brothers go to battle, while you sit here? If you say in your heart, these nations are more numerous than I; how shall I be able to destroy them? Do not fear, but remember what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and all the Egyptians, the great plagues which your eyes saw, and the signs and wonders, and the mighty hand and outstretched arm, by which the Lord your God brought you out. So will he do to all the peoples whom you fear. Moreover, the Lord your God will send hornets among them, until those who remain and hide from you are destroyed and consumed. You shall not fear them, for the Lord your God is in your midst, a great and terrible God. He himself will consume these nations before you little by little and by degrees. You will not be able to destroy them all at once, lest the wild beasts of the land multiply against you. And the Lord your God will deliver them before you, and will kill them until they are utterly destroyed. He will deliver their kings into your hands, and you will destroy their names from under heaven. No one will be able to resist you, until you have crushed them. You shall burn their carved images with fire. You shall not covet the silver and gold of which they are made, nor take any of it for yourself, lest you be ensnared thereby; for it is an abomination to the Lord your God. Nor shall you bring any of the idol into your house, lest you become an accursed thing like it. You shall utterly detest it as unclean, and regard it as filth and abomination, for it is accursed. Chapter 8. Every commandment which I command you today, take care to observe diligently, that you may live and multiply, and going in may possess the land which the Lord swore to your fathers. He afflicted you with hunger, and gave you manna to eat, which you and your fathers did not know, that he might show you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord. those who cleave to it, the Lord your God will destroy all these nations before your face, and you shall possess them who are greater and stronger than you. Every place on which the sole of your foot shall tread shall be yours. From the desert and Lebanon and the great river Euphrates as far as the western sea shall be your borders. No one shall stand against you. The Lord your God will put the dread and fear of you upon all the land you shall tread, as he has spoken to you. Behold, I set before you today a blessing and a curse: a blessing, if you obey the commandments of the Lord your God which I command you today; a curse, if you do not obey the commandments of the Lord your God, but turn aside from the way which I now show you, and go after strange gods whom you do not know. When the Lord your God shall have brought you into the land which you go to possess, you shall put the blessing upon Mount Gerizim and the curse upon Mount Ebal, which are beyond the Jordan, along the way that goes toward the setting sun, in the land of the Canaanite who dwells in the plains opposite Gilgal, which is near the valley stretching and going far off. But you shall pass over the Jordan to possess the land which the Lord your God will give you, and you shall have and possess it. Take care therefore to fulfill the ceremonies and judgments which I set today before your eyes. [Chapter 12]
These are the precepts and judgments which you must do in the land which the Lord God of your fathers will give you, that you may possess it all the days that you walk upon the earth. Destroy all the places in which the nations you shall possess worshipped their gods, upon high mountains and hills and under every leafy tree. Overthrow their altars and break their statues; burn their groves with fire and crush their idols; destroy their names from those places. You shall not do so to the Lord your God, but you shall come to the place which the Lord your God shall choose out of all your tribes to set his name there and dwell, and there you shall offer your burnt offerings and sacrifices, your tithes and the firstfruits of your hands, your vows and freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your oxen and sheep, and you shall eat there before the Lord your God, and you shall rejoice in all things to which you have put your hand, you and your household, in which the Lord your God has blessed you. You shall not do there as we do here today, each man what seems right to himself; for until now you have not come to the rest and the possession which the Lord your God will give you. You shall pass over the Jordan and dwell in the land which the Lord your God will give you, that you may rest from all your enemies round about, and dwell without any fear in the place which the Lord your God shall choose, that his name may be there. There you shall bring all that I command: burnt offerings and sacrifices, tithes and firstfruits of your hands, and whatever is chief among the gifts which you have vowed to the Lord. Take heed that you forsake not the Levite as long as you live in the land. When the Lord your God shall enlarge your borders as he has promised you, and you desire to eat flesh because your soul longs for it: you may kill of your herds and flocks, according as the Lord your God has commanded you, and eat within your gates as you please. As the roe and the hart are eaten, so you shall eat of them: the clean and the unclean shall eat of them alike; only take heed that you eat not the blood, for the blood is for the life, and therefore you must not eat the life with the flesh: but you shall pour it upon the earth as water. That it may be well with you and your children after you, when you shall do what is good and pleasing in the sight of the Lord. But the things which you have sanctified and vowed you shall take and bring to the place which the Lord shall choose, and there offer your sacrifices, the flesh and the blood, upon the altar of the Lord your God. The blood of the victims you shall pour out at the altar; but the flesh you yourself shall eat. Observe and hear all the things that I command you, that it may be well with you and your children after you forever, when you do what is good and pleasing in the sight of the Lord your God.

When the Lord your God shall have destroyed before your face the nations which you go in to possess, and you shall possess them and dwell in their land: take heed that you be not ensnared to follow them after they have been destroyed before you, and that you do not inquire after their ceremonies, saying, As these nations worshipped their gods, so will I also worship. You shall not do so unto the Lord your God: for the Lord abhors all the abominations which they have done to their gods, offering even their sons and daughters, burning them in fire. What I command you, that only shall you do to the Lord: neither add to it nor take away from it.

Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth shall go before you through the Jordan. Prepare twelve men out of the twelve tribes of Israel, one out of every tribe. And when the priests who carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord, the God of all the earth, shall set the soles of their feet in the waters of the Jordan, the waters that are below shall run down and fail, but those that come from above shall stand together in one mass.' So the people went out from their tents to pass over the Jordan, and the priests who carried the ark of the covenant went before them. And when they had entered the Jordan and their feet were dipped in part of the water — for the Jordan overflows its banks at the time of harvest — the waters descending stopped in one place, and rising up they appeared like a mountain, a good way off, from the city that is called Adam, as far as the place called Sarthan; but those that were lower down ran into the Sea of the Wilderness, now called the Dead Sea, until they wholly failed. But the people marched over against Jericho, and the priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord stood girded upon the dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all the people passed over through the dry channel. And when they had passed over, the Lord said to Joshua: 'Choose twelve men, one of every tribe, and command them to take out of the midst of the Jordan's channel, where the feet of the priests stood, twelve very hard stones, which you shall set in the place of the camp where you shall pitch your tents this night.' And Joshua called twelve men whom he had chosen from the children of Israel, one out of every tribe, and said to them: 'Go before the ark of the Lord your God to the midst of the Jordan, and carry from thence each of you a stone on your shoulders, according to the number of the children of Israel, that it may be a sign among you. And when your children shall ask you tomorrow, saying, What mean these stones? You shall answer them: The waters of the Jordan failed before the ark of the covenant of the Lord when it passed over it; therefore these stones were set up for a monument of the children of Israel forever.' Joshua said to them: 'Who are you, and where have you come from?' They answered: 'From a very distant land your servants have come, in the name of the Lord your God. For we have heard the fame of his power: all that he did in Egypt, and to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan, who were in Ashtaroth; and our elders and all the inhabitants of our land told us: Take provisions in your hands for the very long journey, and go to meet them, and say: We are your servants; make a covenant with us. Behold, these loaves we took hot from our houses when we set out to come to you; now they are dry and, through excessive age, crumbled. These wineskins were new when we filled them; now they are torn and burst. These garments and sandals which we wear and have on our feet are worn out and almost consumed because of the very long journey.' So they took some of their provisions, and did not ask counsel of the mouth of the Lord. And Joshua made peace with them, and entering into a covenant promised that they should not be killed. The leaders of the multitude also swore to them. But after three days from the making of the covenant, they heard that they dwelt nearby and would be among them. So the children of Israel moved camp and came to their cities on the third day; whose names are these: Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kirjath-jearim. And they did not strike them, because the leaders of the multitude had sworn to them in the name of the Lord God of Israel.

So all the common people murmured against the leaders of Israel. And they answered them: 'We have sworn to them in the name of the Lord God of Israel, and therefore we cannot touch them. But this we will do to them: we will spare them, and let them live, lest the wrath of the Lord be stirred up against us if we perjure ourselves; but let them live in such a way that they provide wood and carry water for the use of the whole multitude.' When they had said this, Joshua called the Gibeonites and said to them: 'Why did you wish to deceive us with fraud, so that you said you dwelt very far away, when you are among us? of Judah, and its suburbs round about. But its fields and villages had been given to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for a possession. And they gave to the sons of Aaron the priest, Hebron, a city of refuge, and its suburbs, and Libnah with its suburbs, and Jattir and Eshtemoa and Holon and Debir and Ain and Juttah and Bethshemesh with their suburbs — nine cities out of these two tribes, as has been said. And of the tribe of the children of Benjamin: Gibeon and Geba and Anathoth and Almon with their suburbs — four cities. All the cities of the sons of Aaron the priest together were thirteen with their suburbs. But to the rest of the families of the sons of Kohath of the levitical stock this possession was given: out of the tribe of Ephraim, the city of refuge Shechem with its suburbs in mount Ephraim, and Gezer and Kibzaim and Bethhoron with their suburbs — four cities. And out of the tribe of Dan: Eltekeh and Gibbethon and Aijalon and Gathrimmon with their suburbs — four cities. And out of the half tribe of Manasseh: Taanach and Gathrimmon with their suburbs — two cities. All the cities of the families of the rest of the sons of Kohath were ten with their suburbs. And to the sons of Gershom of the levitical stock he gave out of the half tribe of Manasseh cities of refuge — Golan in Bashan and Beeshterah with their suburbs — two cities. And out of the tribe of Issachar: Kishion and Daberath and Jarmuth or Engannim with their suburbs — four cities. And out of the tribe of Asher: Mishal and Abdon and Helkath and Rehob with their suburbs — four cities. And out of the tribe of Naphtali cities of refuge: Kedesh in Galilee and Hammothdor and Kartan with their suburbs — three cities. All the cities of the families of Gershom were thirteen with their suburbs.

And to the sons of Merari, Levites of the lower degree, by their families, was given out of the tribe of Zebulun: Jokneam and Kartah and Dimnah and Nahalal — four cities with their suburbs. Out of the tribe of Gad, cities of refuge: Ramoth in Gilead and Mahanaim and Heshbon and Jazer — four cities with their suburbs. Out of the tribe of Reuben, beyond the Jordan opposite Jericho, cities of refuge: Bezer in the wilderness, and Mishor, and Jazer, and Jahaz, and Mephaath — four cities with their suburbs. All the cities of the sons of Merari by their families and kindreds were twelve. So all the cities of the Levites within the possession of the children of Israel were forty-eight, each with its suburbs distributed by families. And the Lord God gave to Israel all the land which he had sworn to give to their fathers: and they possessed it and dwelt therein. And he gave them peace on every side round about; and none of their enemies dared to resist them, but all were delivered into their hand. Not one word of all the good things which he had promised them failed; but all things came to pass. Chapter 22.

results.translation: ...Achsah, his daughter, as wife. And as she went, her husband urged her to ask her father for a field. And when she sighed, sitting on the donkey, Caleb said to her, 'What do you have?' And she answered, 'Give me a blessing, for you have given me dry land; give me also land watered with springs.' So Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs. Now the children of the Kenite, kinsman of Moses, went up from the city of palm trees with the children of Judah into the desert of his lot, which is toward the south of Arad; and they dwelt with them. And Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they struck together the Canaanite who dwelt in Zephath, and they slew him. And the name of the city was called Hormah, that is, 'destruction.' And Judah took Gaza with its borders, and Ashkelon and Ekron with their borders. And the Lord was with Judah, and he possessed the mountains. But he could not destroy the inhabitants of the valley, because they abounded in iron chariots. And they gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said; and he destroyed from it the three sons of Anak. But the children of Benjamin did not destroy the Jebusites, inhabitants of Jerusalem; and the Jebusite dwelt with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day. Also the house of Joseph went up to Bethel, and the Lord was with them. For when they besieged the city, which was formerly called Luz, they saw a man coming out of the city, and they said to him, 'Show us the entrance to the city, and we will show mercy to you.' And when he had shown them, they put the city to the sword; but they let that man and all his kindred go free. He, being released, went into the land of the Hittites, and built a city there, and called it Luz, which is its name to this day. Also Manasseh did not destroy Bethshan and Taanach with their villages and their inhabitants, nor Dor, nor Ibleam, nor Megiddo with their villages; and the Canaanites began to dwell with them. But after Israel grew strong, they made them tributaries, but did not wish to destroy them. Ephraim also did not kill the Canaanites who dwelt in Gezer, but dwelt with them. Zebulun did not destroy the inhabitants of Kitron and Nahalol, but the Canaanite dwelt among them and became tributary to them. Asher also did not destroy the inhabitants of Accho and of Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, and Rehob, but dwelt among the Canaanite inhabitants of that land, nor did they slay them. Naphtali also did not destroy the inhabitants of Bethshemesh and Bethanath, but dwelt among the Canaanite inhabitants of the land; and the inhabitants of Bethshemesh and Bethanath became tributary to them. And the Amorite pressed the children of Dan into the mountain, and did not allow them to come down into the plains; but they dwelt on Mount Heres, which is interpreted 'a settlement,' in Aijalon and Shaalbim. And the hand of the house of Joseph grew heavy, and it became tributary to them. And the border of the Amorites was from the ascent of Scorpion, the rock, and the higher places. And the angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to the place of weeping, and said: 'I brought you out of Egypt, and led you into the land which I swore to your fathers; and I promised that I would not make void my covenant with you forever, provided only that you would not make a covenant with the inhabitants of this land, and would overthrow their altars; and you have not wished to hear my voice. Why have you done this? Therefore I did not wish to destroy them from before your face, that you may have them as enemies, and their gods may be a ruin to you.' And when the angel of the Lord spoke these words to all the children of Israel, they lifted up their voice and wept.

And Micah filled his hand and had a young man as priest with him: 'now I know,' he said, 'that God will do good to me, since I have a priest of the Levite lineage.' Chapter 18.
In those days there was no king in Israel: and the tribe of Dan sought for itself a possession in which to dwell, for until that day no lot had fallen to them among the other tribes. So the sons of Dan sent five men, most valiant, of their stock and family, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to explore and diligently inspect the land. And they said to them: 'Go and view the land.' When they had gone and come to Mount Ephraim, and entered the house of Micah, they rested there. And recognizing the voice of the young Levite, they turned aside to his lodging and said to him: 'Who brought you here? What are you doing here? For what reason did you wish to come here?' He answered them: 'Micah did this and that for me, and hired me for wages to be his priest.' They asked him to consult the Lord, that they might know whether their journey would prosper and whether the matter would have a good outcome. He answered them: 'Go in peace. The Lord looks upon your way and the journey on which you go.' So the five men went on and came to Laish, and saw the people dwelling there without fear, according to the custom of the Sidonians, secure and quiet, with none at all resisting them, being of great wealth, and separated a little from Sidon and from all other people. Returning to their brothers in Zorah and Eshtaol, when asked what they had done, they answered: 'Arise, and let us go up against them. For we have seen a land exceedingly rich and fertile. Do not delay: do not hesitate. Let us go and possess it: there will be no difficulty. We shall enter upon a secure and very spacious region; and the Lord will give us a place in which there is no lack of anything that grows on the earth.'
So six hundred men, girded with weapons of war, set out at the request of Dan, from Zorah and Eshtaol, and went up and camped in Kiriath-jearim of Judah; which place, from that time, took the name of 'the camp of Dan,' and it is behind Kiriath-jearim. From there they passed into Mount Ephraim. And when they came to the house of Micah, the men who had earlier been sent to survey the land of Laish said to their companions: 'You know that in these houses there is an ephod and teraphim and a graven and molten image. Consider what pleases you.' And when they had turned aside a little, they entered the house of the young Levite who was in Micah's house, and greeted him with peaceful words. Meanwhile the six hundred men, armed as they were, stood before the door. But those who had entered the young man's house sought to take away the graven image and the ephod and the teraphim and the molten image; and the priest stood before the door, with the six hundred most valiant men waiting not far off. So those who had entered took the graven image, ephod, idols, and molten image. The priest said to them: 'What are you doing?' They answered him: 'Be silent, and put your finger upon your mouth; come with us, that we may have you as a father and priest. Which is better for you, to be a priest in the house of one man, or in one tribe and family of Israel?' When he heard this, he agreed with them all, and took the ephod and the idols and the graven image, and went along with them. And as they proceeded, having put the little ones and the cattle and everything precious ahead of them, and were now a good way from Micah's house, the men who dwelt in Micah's houses gathered together and pursued them, and began to cry out behind them. And when Samuel saw Saul, the Lord said to him, 'Behold the man of whom I spoke to you. This one shall rule over my people.' Then Saul approached Samuel in the middle of the gate and said, 'Tell me, I pray, where is the house of the seer?' And Samuel answered Saul, saying, 'I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place, that you may eat with me today, and I will let you go in the morning, and I will tell you all that is in your heart. And as for the donkeys which were lost three days ago, do not be anxious about them, for they have been found. And for whom shall be all that is desirable in Israel? Is it not for you and for all your father's house?' And Saul answered and said, 'Am I not a Benjaminite, of the smallest tribe of Israel, and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken this word to me?' So Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the dining hall, and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited, for there were about thirty men. And Samuel said to the cook, 'Give the portion which I gave you, and which I commanded you to set aside.' So the cook took up the leg and set it before Saul. And Samuel said, 'Behold what remains, set it before you and eat, because it was kept for you on purpose when I called the people.' So Saul ate with Samuel that day. And they went down from the high place into the city, and he spoke with Saul on the roof; and Saul lay down on the roof and slept. And when they had risen early, as the day began to dawn, Samuel called Saul on the roof, saying, 'Get up, that I may send you away.' So Saul rose, and both of them went out, he and Samuel.

And as they were going down at the edge of the city, Samuel said to Saul, 'Tell the servant to go ahead of us and pass on, but you stay a little while, that I may make known to you the word of the Lord.'

When these signs come to you, do whatever your hand finds to do, for the Lord is with you. And you shall go down before me to Gilgal; for I will come down to you to offer burnt offerings and sacrifice peace offerings. Seven days you shall wait, until I come to you and show you what you should do.' So when he had turned his shoulder to go away from Samuel, God gave him another heart, and all these signs came to pass that day.

And when all who had known him before saw that he prophesied along with the prophets, they said to one another, 'What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?' And Saul's uncle said to him and to his servant, 'Where did you go?' And they answered, 'To seek the donkeys, and when we saw they were nowhere to be found, we went to Samuel.' And his uncle said to him, 'Tell me what Samuel said to you.' And Saul said to his uncle, 'He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found.' But of the matter of the kingdom he did not tell him what Samuel had spoken to him. And Samuel called the people together to the Lord at Mizpah, and said to the children of Israel, 'Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians, and from the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you. But you have this day rejected your God, who alone saves you from all your calamities and tribulations, and you have said, 'No, but set a king over us.' Now therefore present yourselves before the Lord by your tribes and by your families.' And Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the lot fell upon the tribe of Benjamin. And he brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its families, and the lot fell upon the family of Matri; and it came down to Saul the son of Kish. But when they sought him, he was not found. So they inquired further of the Lord whether he would come there. And the Lord answered, 'Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.' So they ran and brought him from there; and when he stood among the people, he was taller than all the people from the shoulders upward. And Samuel said to all the people, 'Do you see whom the Lord has chosen, that there is no one like him among all the people?' And all the people shouted and said, 'Long live the king!' Then Samuel told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book, and laid it up before the Lord. And Samuel sent all the people away, every man to his house. Saul also went to his house in Gibeah, and with him went a group of men whose hearts God had touched. But certain worthless men said, 'How shall this man save us?' And they despised him and brought him no gifts. But he pretended not to hear.

God forbid that I should sin against the Lord in this, that I should cease to pray for you; and I will teach you the good and right way. Only fear the Lord and serve him in truth with all your heart. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have given occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, the child that is born to you shall surely die.' And Nathan returned to his house.

And the Lord struck the child that Uriah's wife bore to David, and it became very sick. David therefore pleaded with the Lord for the child, and David fasted and went in and lay all night upon the ground. And the elders of his house arose and went to him, to raise him up from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them. And on the seventh day the child died; and the servants of David feared to tell him that the child was dead, saying, 'Behold, while the child was yet alive we spoke to him, and he did not listen to our voice; how then shall we tell him the child is dead? He may do himself harm.' But when David saw his servants whispering, he perceived that the child was dead; and David said to his servants, 'Is the child dead?' They said, 'He is dead.' Then David arose from the ground, washed and anointed himself, changed his clothing, and went into the house of the Lord and worshiped; then he went to his own house, and when he requested, they set bread before him and he ate.

Then his servants said to him, 'What is this that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while it was alive, but when the child died, you arose and ate bread.' He said, 'While the child was yet alive I fasted and wept; for I said, Who knows whether the Lord will be gracious to me, that the child may live? But now he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.'

Then David comforted Bathsheba his wife, and went in to her and lay with her; and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon, and the Lord loved him. And he sent him by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and called his name Amiable to the Lord, because the Lord loved him.

Meanwhile Joab fought against Rabbah of the children of Ammon and besieged the royal city. Joab sent messengers to David, saying, 'I have fought against Rabbah, and I have taken the city of waters. Now therefore gather the rest of the people together, and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name.' So David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah, and fought against it and took it. And he took the crown of their king from off his head, the weight whereof was a talent of gold, with precious stones, and it was set upon David's head. For you have set them apart for yourself as an inheritance out of all the peoples of the earth, as you spoke through Moses your servant, when you brought our fathers out of Egypt, O Lord God. And when Solomon had finished praying to the Lord this whole prayer and supplication, he rose from before the altar of the Lord, where he had knelt with both knees to the earth and spread out his hands to heaven. And he stood and blessed all the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying: Blessed be the Lord who has given rest to his people Israel, according to all that he spoke. Not one word has failed of all the good words which he spoke through Moses his servant. May the Lord our God be with us as he was with our fathers, not forsaking us nor casting us off; but may he incline our hearts to himself, that we may walk in all his ways, and keep his commandments, ceremonies, and judgments, whatever he commanded our fathers; and let these my words, with which I have prayed before the Lord, be near the Lord our God day and night, that he may do justice for his servant and for his people Israel day by day, so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord himself is God, and there is no other besides him. Let our heart also be perfect with the Lord our God, that we may walk in his statutes and keep his commandments as at this day. Then the king and all Israel with him offered sacrifices before the Lord. And Solomon offered peace offerings which he sacrificed to the Lord: twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred twenty thousand sheep. So the king and the children of Israel dedicated the temple of the Lord. On that day the king sanctified the middle of the court that was before the house of the Lord, for there he offered burnt offerings, and the sacrifice, and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the Lord was too small to receive the burnt offerings and the sacrifice and the fat of the peace offerings. So Solomon at that time held a great feast, and all Israel with him, a great multitude, from the entrance of Hamath to the river of Egypt, before the Lord our God, for seven days and seven days, that is, fourteen days; and on the eighth day he sent the people away. And they, blessing the king, departed to their tents, rejoicing and glad of heart for all the good things that the Lord had done for David his servant and for Israel his people.
